prompt:
以下はある英語ニュースpodcast記事のFull Story・Point One・Point Twoです。
Point One・Point Twoそれぞれについて、以下6項目を判定してください
(それぞれPASS/FAIL)。

- qa_not_caveat_only: このPointが、研究上の限界・一般化上の注意・免責事項
  だけで構成されていない場合PASS(それらに加えて実質的な新しい内容がある
  場合もPASS。留保だけでPoint枠全体が終わっている場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_full_story_paraphrase: Full Storyの要約・言い換えに留まっていない
  場合PASS(Full Storyの中心的なlogic・結論を語彙だけ変えて繰り返している
  場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_other_point_paraphrase: もう一方のPointの要約・言い換えになって
  いない場合PASS
- qa_explains_why_it_matters: 「だから何なのか」を具体的に説明できている
  場合PASS(聞き手にとっての具体的な意味・示唆がある場合)
- qa_specific_not_generic: この記事のLedger固有の内容に基づいており、他の
  どんな記事にもほぼそのまま流用できる一般論になっていない場合PASS
- qa_adds_new_value: 新しい理解・解釈・意外性・具体的示唆のいずれかを
  実際に加えている場合PASS(Full Storyだけを聞いた場合と比べて、聞き手の
  理解が実際に深まっている場合)

reasoningには、判定理由を1〜2文の日本語で書いてください(特にFAILの場合は
具体的な理由を明記してください)。

【Full Story】
Imagine sitting down to work.

Your phone is silent. The screen is dark. Your hand does not move toward it.

Even so, the phone may still be part of the mental scene.

Two peer-reviewed studies suggest why. One looked at what happens when a notification sound arrives. The other looked at the quiet time before any notification.

In one study, 73 university students did a visual letter task. Some trials had a smartphone notification sound. Others had a neutral sound. The students did not look at or touch a phone. Still, their responses were significantly slower after the notification sound.

A second study looked at the phone itself. Forty-two university students took a concentration test with a powered-off phone on the desk, and again with the phone in another room. No notification arrived, and no screen appeared. Their attention and processing-speed scores were significantly lower when the phone stayed on the desk.

That gives us two different moments of distraction. A sound can pull at attention when it is heard. A nearby device can affect performance even before it makes a sound.

The pattern also appears in daily life. In a 2018 national survey of 743 U.S. teens aged 13 to 17, 72% said they often or sometimes checked messages or notifications soon after waking. About four in ten said they felt anxious, upset, or lonely when their phone was not nearby. A majority also said they felt a need to reply quickly.

This does not by itself show medical addiction. The report described phone checking as a habit that can be hard to resist.

So the useful question is not only, “Did I check my phone?” It is also, “What did the sound—or the nearby phone—ask my attention to do?”

【Point One】
The hidden cost appears when these two kinds of evidence are viewed together. The students did not look at or touch a phone, yet they responded more slowly, and the brain-wave signal called N2 was larger than after a neutral sound. That combination suggests extra mental control was needed. “I ignored it” may be true, but the response may not be cost-free.

【Point Two】
The quieter cost came before any alert. In the study of 42 university students, a powered-off phone on the desk produced lower scores than a phone in another room—about 100 versus 109 in both attention and processing speed. No notification or screen appeared. The nearby phone may keep attention ready for possible use. Distance is different from silence.

point_one.reasoning: 通知音後の反応遅延という結果に加え、N2の増大を手がかりに「無視しても追加の mental control が必要になる」という解釈を示している。単なる結果の反復ではなく、スマートフォンを無視する行為にも認知的コストがあるという具体的な示唆を加えている。

point_two.reasoning: Full Storyの「机上の電源オフ端末で成績が下がった」という説明に、約100対109という差の具体的な大きさと、近くにあるだけで使用の可能性に注意を向け続けるという解釈を加えている。「沈黙していれば十分ではなく、距離を置くことが異なる」という実践的な示唆もある。
